extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of literary criticism and poetry (Victorian/English literature readers and critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for evaluating and producing poetry and literary criticism (definitions like 'grand style', the purpose of literature, qualities of competent criticism, relations to classical models). Geared to readers and critics considering poetic form, tone, purpose, and the ethics of criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grand style
rubrics_metrics.description: The grand style arises in poetry when a noble nature, poetically gifted, treats with simplicity or with severity a serious subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold admits the term 'grand style' is incapable of exact verbal definition but characterizes it by the combination of a noble poet and the manner of treatment (simplicity or severity) of a serious subject. (See his reference in 'On Translating Homer'.) Guidance: aim for nobility of nature and serious subject-matter expressed with simplicity/severity; anti-patterns include affectation, excessive ornament, or trivial subjects dressed up with pretension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature's purpose — 'a criticism of life'
rubrics_metrics.description: The end and aim of all literature, if one considers it attentively, is, in truth, nothing but a criticism of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arnold asserts that literature (and especially poetry) should function as a 'criticism of life' — i.e., it should examine, interpret, or judge human life and conduct. Guidance: works should illuminate moral, social, or spiritual dimensions of life; anti-patterns include purely decorative writing with no reflective or evaluative engagement with life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence and fitness of the critic/introduction writer
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices or introductions to eminent authors' works should be by a competent critic — 'a man of letters, not, as too often happens, some relation or friend with no qualification for his task except affection for his author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial/introductory material should be written by someone qualified to judge and contextualize the work. Guidance: prefer introductions by critics who are knowledgeable and critical rather than by acquaintances; anti-pattern: sentimental or unqualified puff pieces presented as authoritative criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of personal attack in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold states a strong dislike of personal attack and controversy and, in practice, abstains from reprinting personal attacks he once published; he prefers criticism that is not merely personal denunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical practice should avoid ad hominem attacks and sustained personal controversy; guidance: focus on ideas, methods, and texts rather than personalities; exception/qualification: measured critique of ideas grounded in argument is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philistinism as a negative evaluative category
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Philistine' denotes a person devoid of culture and enlightenment, swayed chiefly by material interests and blind to the force of ideas and the value of culture — a recurrent negative criterion in Arnold's judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'philistinism' to diagnose and critique work or social attitudes that prioritize utility, material show, or publicity over cultural and intellectual values. Anti-patterns: treating popularity or commercial success as equivalent to cultural worth without attention to ideas, depth, or form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry and studies should ennoble the soul (impress virtues)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted from Plato and Arnold's references: favor studies and works which 'impress' qualities like justice, temperance, and wisdom on the soul; criticism should value works that perfect and ennoble the spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing poetry and literature, give weight to the work's capacity to cultivate moral or intellectual virtues. Guidance: prefer works that elevate the reader's character or understanding; anti-patterns include works that merely titillate or flatter without moral or intellectual substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of form and learning from classical models
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold's notes repeatedly reference classical models (Homer, Dante, Virgil, Chaucer, Dryden, etc.) and technical matters (stanza forms, meter) indicating that mastery of form and acquaintance with classical models are standards for poetic excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers of poetry should study classical models and forms (e.g., stanza types, heroic verse, grand themes) and show technical command. Guidance: imitation and adaptation of great models (when done intelligently) is a virtue; anti-patterns include sloppy meter, ignorance of poetic forms, or willful rejection of craft that weakens expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation should preserve the 'grand style' and the seriousness of subject
rubrics_metrics.description: In the context of 'On Translating Homer' and Arnold's comments, translation should seek to render the original's grand style: the noble treatment of serious subjects with appropriate simplicity or severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translators should aim not just for literal accuracy but for recreating the aesthetic tone and moral seriousness of the original. Guidance: prioritize tone, dignity, and stylistic effect appropriate to the source; anti-patterns include literalistic renderings that lose nobility or trivialize the original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detachment and dispassionate judgment in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit in Arnold's discussion (and the footnote on 'detachment'): criticism benefits from an attitude of detachment — emancipation from crude cravings and passions — to judge literature more fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should cultivate detachment (avoid excessive personal bias, factionalism, or party spirit) to see works 'as they really are.' Guidance: favor calm, balanced evaluation; anti-patterns include sectarian polemics, partisan praise/denunciation, or criticism clouded by personal animus.
